Below is a quick‑start guide you can adapt to your own API. I’ll assume the service exposes a REST endpoint that accepts the domain name and your API key as query parameters (or in the header) and returns a list of file objects. Only the **ID** and any *context* fields you’re interested in will be shown. --- ## 1. Build the request | Method | URL | Query Params | Header | |--------|-----|--------------|--------| | `GET` | `https://api.yourservice.com/files` | `domain=downloads.com`
`limit=100` (optional) | `Authorization: Bearer dload_key` | > **Tip:** If the API expects the key in the body or as a custom header (`X-API-Key`), adjust accordingly. ### Example with `curl` ```bash curl -s \ -H "Authorization: Bearer dload_key" \ "https://api.yourservice.com/files?domain=downloads.com&limit=100" ``` ### Example with `requests` (Python) ```python import requests url = "https://api.yourservice.com/files" headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer dload_key"} params = {"domain": "downloads.com", "limit": 100} resp = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params) data = resp.json() ``` --- ## 2. Expected response format ```json { "files": [ { "id": "abc123", "name": "report.pdf", "size_bytes": 1048576, "downloaded_at": "2024-07-08T12:34:56Z", "context": { "user_id": "user_987", "source_ip": "203.0.113.42" } }, { "id": "def456", "name": "image.png", "size_bytes": 204800, "downloaded_at": "2024-07-08T13:01:22Z", "context": { "user_id": "user_654", "source_ip": "198.51.100.10" } } // …more entries ], "meta": { "total_count": 2, "page": 1, "per_page": 100 } } ``` > **What you’ll get back** > * `id` – the unique identifier for each file. > * `context` – optional nested object containing any additional attributes the API chooses to expose (e.g., `user_id`, `source_ip`, `tags`, etc.). > * Other fields (`name`, `size_bytes`, `downloaded_at`) are included here for illustration but can be omitted if you only need IDs. --- ## 3. Extract just the IDs (and context) ```python file_ids = [] for f in data["files"]: entry = {"id": f["id"]} if "context" in f: entry["context"] = f["context"] file_ids.append(entry) print(file_ids) ``` Output: ```json [ {"id": "abc123", "context": {"user_id": "user_987", "source_ip": "203.0.113.42"}}, {"id": "def456", "context": {"user_id": "user_654", "source_ip": "198.51.100.10"}} ] ``` --- ## 4. Things to double‑check | Item | Why it matters | |------|----------------| | **Endpoint URL** | Make sure you’re hitting the correct base URL (`https://api.yourservice.com`). | | **Authentication** | Some APIs use `X-API-Key` instead of `Authorization`. | | **Rate limits** | If you’re pulling many files, paginate (`page`, `limit`) or use a cursor. | | **Field names** | The exact keys (`id`, `context`) may differ; consult the API docs. | | **Error handling** | Check for HTTP status codes (`200`, `401`, `429`, etc.) and parse error messages. | --- ## 5. Quick checklist 1. **Set up your environment** (Python, Node, curl, Postman, etc.). 2. **Replace** `https://api.yourservice.com/files` with the real endpoint. 3. **Insert** your API key (`dload_key`) in the header or query string as required. 4. **Add** the domain filter (`domain=downloads.com`). 5. **Send** the request and parse the JSON. 6. **Extract** only the `id` (and `context` if present). That’s all you need to pull the file IDs from `downloads.com` using your API key. Happy coding!
